narrative: Your promotion is being denied because the model estimates a 47.0% chance that you will leave the organization. That is not a certainty, but it is high enough to mark you as a retention risk, and the promotion process treats that risk as a reason to pause advancement. The strongest factor in the assessment was your overall experience: one to five years, a range shared by about half of employees who stay, so this actually counted in your favor and suggested stability. The next factor, and the main push toward leaving, was that you reported other job opportunities. Only about one in four otherwise stable employees said they had outside options, so your yes makes departure look more plausible. The third factor was training: you attended one to three programs in the last three years. While not unusual, it still slightly increased the leave signal, perhaps because it suggests you are building skills that could be attractive elsewhere or because more development was expected. Other profile details—modest salary, no medical insurance, no bonus, unpaid overtime, pay dissatisfaction and not feeling you received the promotion you deserved—add to the concern. To change this outcome, consider discussing retention supports, clearer promotion criteria, compensation, benefits, and development with your manager. The organization should review whether denying promotion to someone with outside options increases the very leave risk it fears.
